text:
maya: Heads-up — since 09:12 UTC we're seeing a flurry of ALB target deregistrations from the us-west-2 edge GPU fleet. Targets go unhealthy then re-register 20-40s later. Not seeing pod restarts.
ashwin: I can see the spike in ALB 502/connection resets in the logs. Happening across ~6 nodes, all in same private subnet. Logs:
ashwin: ```ALB: health check failed -> connection reset by peer
[k8s] probe: GET /healthz -> ECONNRESET from 10.0.45.123:443
``` 
ben: Any recent kube-proxy or node kernel upgrades? SNAT port exhaustion maybe? 502s + quick re-registration smells like SNAT churn.
lucy: No infra deploys since last night. We did scale up some inference jobs on the GPU pool earlier today so egress NAT usage could be much higher.
maya: Timeline: spike started around 09:12 when a batch of GPU pods kicked off heavy model pulls/telemetry egress. ALB healthchecks are TCP/HTTP from the ALB subnets to pod IPs (target-type=ip). We rely on SNAT for pod->alb return path.
ashwin: I pulled conntrack + iptables stats from affected nodes:

ashwin: ```
# conntrack -S
found 65536 flow entries
# ss -s
TCP: 12345 (estab 12000, timewait 1500)
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_conntrack_max
65536
``` 
ben: That conntrack ceiling + increased outbound flows could cause ephemeral port reuse/rotation. If ALB probe responses are SNAT'ed out different IPs or ports, ALB sees resets and marks unhealthy.
lucy: Also noticed SNAT port allocation dip on one node where many pods did model downloads to S3 concurrently. NAT Gateway metrics show short-lived quota spikes.
maya: Quick checks on ALB logs show health check source IPs alternating but some SYNs never complete. Packet capture from node shows FIN/RST after SNAT translation changed.
ashwin: Repro steps I ran locally: saturate outbound with curl loops and simultaneously hit ALB health endpoint -> health failures after ephemeral port churn ~60s.
ben: Short term mitigation options?
ben: 1) Move the service's ALB target-type to "instance" so that healthchecks hit node IPs (avoids SNAT for checks) 2) Increase NAT capacity (additional NAT GW or use NAT GW per AZ) 3) Configure egress to use EIPs per node (AWS NAT mode) 4) Reduce concurrent outbound flows from GPU pods via job rate limiting
lucy: 1) is fastest; we can flip target-type for that TG but need to validate routing and security groups. 2) requires infra change but helpful long-term. 3) needs node-level changes and is heavier.
maya: I suggest quick experiment: change target group to instance for the problematic service and monitor. If that stabilizes, schedule a NAT capacity increase and long-term architecture discussion.
oncall-bot: Incident created: INC-2026-4582. Pager: oncall@redwood. Priority: P2.
ashwin: I applied TG change in staging and reproduced the heavy egress test — healthcheck flap went away almost immediately. POC looks good.
ben: OK if staging looks promising let's do a controlled change in prod for that TG: set target-type=instance + increase healthcheck threshold to 5/10s for extra safety during rollout.
lucy: Will open PR for TG switch + rollout playbook. Also adding a node-level egress throttling config for the GPU batch jobs to avoid repeating.
maya: After switching TG in prod at 09:58 UTC we saw deregistration events stop. ALB UnhealthyCount -> 0 within 2 min. NAT GW 95th percentile still high but stable.
ashwin: Follow-ups:
- Evaluate NAT Gateway autoscaling or add per-AZ NAT GW
- Consider moving high-egress workloads to subnets with dedicated egress
- Audit other IP-target-type services for similar exposure
ben: I'll draft runbook: detection signals (ALB 5xx spikes, conntrack nearing max, TG deregisters), quick remediation (TG->instance, throttle jobs), and long-term plans.
lucy: PR for TG change + rollout tests: https://git.internal/r/infra/tg-instance-rollout
maya: Thanks all. Leaving the incident open until NAT capacity decision is made. :thumbsup:
